How much can you get for your old, discontinued Apple Watch?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your old Apple Watch might still be worth some cash when you trade it in for a new one.
  • The Apple Watch has become a must-have device for many people, and it can last for years.
  • In a recent development, that might make you wonder what you should do with an old, discontinued Apple Watch that you no longer use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your old Apple Watch might still be worth some cash when you trade it in for a new one.

The Apple Watch has become a must-have device for many people, and it can last for years. Chances are that you'll probably buy a new watch before your current one stops working. Still, your old Apple Watch will eventually stop getting software updates — that's what happened this year with watchOS 27, which dropped support for models older than the Series 9. Some of them still get security patches, but the latest features are exclusive to newer devices.

In a recent development, that might make you wonder what you should do with an old, discontinued Apple Watch that you no longer use. Even if you have a legacy Apple Watch, you can resell it or use it for trade-in credit at Apple. They aren't worth much, but it's better than leaving them unused in a drawer to gather dust.

Sources indicate that if you don't want to deal with the hassle of selling your old Apple Watch on your own, the Apple Trade In program is the easiest path. With this, you give your used Apple Watch to Apple and you get credit toward a new product in return — that could be another Apple Watch or anything else, like AirPods or even an iPhone.

Industry observers note that apple regularly updates its trade-in pricing table; at the time of writing, you can get as much as $430 in credit for an Apple Watch. The credit amount depends on the model you have and its condition, like whether it's in good shape or has scratches and cracks. If your Apple Watch is an especially old model or badly damaged, Apple won't offer trade-in credit for it, but it still offers free recycling.

Trade-in values start at up to $30 for the first-generation Apple Watch SE, which came out in 2020. An Apple Watch Series 8 is worth $90 max, while a Series 11 is worth up to $200. The Ultra offers the highest trade-in value: Apple pays up to $430 for a used Apple Watch Ultra 3 in good condition. So for example, if you have a Series 8 in good condition and trade it in for a fresh Apple Watch Series 12 (which starts at $399), the price drops to $309 instead.

Industry observers note that keep in mind that Apple doesn't pay cash for trade-in products. If you don't proposal on buying a newly introduced product right away, or want the credit for something else, you can receive the value as an Apple gift card instead. It's thus a good way to cover the cost of apps or subscriptions.

Recent findings suggest that you can bring your old watch to an Apple Store or mail it in — all shipping costs are covered. Apple adds your trade-in credit to your account balance as soon as it receives your watch and confirms that everything is in order.

Selling an old Apple Watch on your own takes more effort, but also pays you more. On Swappa, a marketplace for used tech, a Series 6 can be worth around $100 — more than double the $45 Apple offers for it. The same applies to other models, like the Series 8, which is worth around $130.

It has been revealed that the amount you can get will depend on which device you have and its condition. Apple Watch models with cellular connectivity and more premium materials, such as steel or titanium, tend to hold their value better than GPS-only and aluminum ones. Just remember to unpair and reset your Apple Watch before trading it in or selling it. Otherwise, Activation Lock will remain enabled, and the buyer won't be able to unlock it without your Apple Account and password. Apple refuses devices with Activation Lock enabled.

And if you decide to keep your old Apple Watch after all, there are some interesting ways to put an older smartwatch to good use, like turning it into your sleep tracker while your main watch charges overnight.

Tesla’s self-driving tech is awaiting another major vote from the European Union before the end of the year.

Italy's Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport has granted provisional approval for Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised), which has been rebranded to Tesla Assisted Driving in Europe. The Tesla Europe account on X confirmed in a post that it's been approved in Italy, with the rollout beginning soon. It also showed off footage of Tesla Assisted Driving operating near The Coliseum and on Italian roads. Italy's minister of infrastucture and transport, Matteo Salvini, also posted on X that Tesla's driver assistance system has been given the green light after a "timely technical feasibility review.".

Sources indicate that italy's approval notches another regulatory milestone for Tesla since the country decided to preempt the European Union's expected vote on its driver assistance system slated for later this year. Tesla is still awaiting decisions from other major European Union countries, including Germany and France, which is currently in the process of testing Tesla Assisted Driving.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Panel-only chargers, built-in batteries and portable power stations all work differently, so here's how to find the right fit.

Industry observers note that when you're out hiking, far away from an electrical outlet or stuck in a power outage, having a backup power bank for your phone and other devices makes sense. But a power bank will eventually run out, possibly leaving you with a phone battery in the red. If you're looking to prevent the inevitable panic that comes with a dead phone, a solar panel charger might be an option for you.

It has been revealed that while there's a whole range of solar-powered chargers on the market, you can find smaller, lighter ones that can recharge devices like phones and laptops. They might be a good fit, particularly if you're on the move. You'll have a few decisions to make about the type of charger that works best for you, as well as the features you'll want, like charging ports and safety protections. Whether you're heading out on a camping trip or just looking to bypass the electrical grid, here's what you need to know about charging your phone with a portable solar charger.

According to recent reports, there are several types of solar-powered charging devices to pick from, and the one you get will largely depend on what you're going to use it for. A panel-only charger lets you plug a device like a phone directly into it. The panels convert sunlight into power, but there's no other way to store that power once it's been captured. A panel-only charger might be better suited for shorter-term use, particularly if it's sunny out.

Other chargers come with built-in batteries, so you can store energy and use it later, creating an extra layer of convenience. If you're camping for a few days, for example, this duo of panels and battery could make it easier to stay charged and give you more control of when you do the charging.

Recent findings suggest that finally, you can spring for a portable power station. While different models will have different features and capacities, a power station will generally let you charge several devices at the same time. It will also have battery storage. It may not be as easy to tote around as the others, but there are some compact units on the market weighing as little as 4 pounds.

Sources indicate that when you're deciding on a portable solar charger, there are a few considerations you want to make. For one, there's wattage. A model that's smaller and lighter-weight might be able to produce 15-50 watts. This range should work fine for charging smaller devices like your phone. It's important to remember that the wattage will be impacted by variables like cloud cover or how the device is angled toward the sun, so you might not always get the wattage listed on the packaging. These factors will change charging time too.

Sources indicate that in addition, consider the number of ports that come with a portable solar charger. Some solar panel chargers will let you plug your phone directly into them with a USB-C port. Also think about how you'll be using it. A bigger, bulkier solar charging device might be harder to lug around if you're camping or hiking. Some chargers fold, making them easier to carry, or have stands that will help you better position the panels toward the sun. Others can clip to a backpack. Finally, be mindful of safety features like water and weather resistance, overcharge protection and temperature control.

Six simple Raspberry Pi projects for beginners

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stop leaving your Pi builds unfinished with these fun and useful ideas.
  • Industry observers note that raspberry Pi projects are infamous for fizzling out before completion.
  • In a recent development, even Raspberry Pis haven't been spared from RAMageddon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stop leaving your Pi builds unfinished with these fun and useful ideas.

Industry observers note that raspberry Pi projects are infamous for fizzling out before completion. Sure, the truly dedicated will finish things like custom voice assistants, irrigation systems or creepy animatronics. However, many Pi projects end up requiring more patience than beginners are willing to invest. Here are a few ideas that should be easy enough to prevent your purchase from collecting dust.

In a recent development, even Raspberry Pis haven't been spared from RAMageddon. With AI data centers gobbling up the world's memory supply, we've seen several Pi price increases since late 2025. The 16GB Pi 5 now costs $385, over three times its original $120 MSRP. A Pi is no longer the impulse purchase it once was.

Recent findings suggest that mini PCs also fell victim to the RAM crisis, but they're still worth considering for some projects. A fully loaded Pi can cost at least as much as a small Intel mini PC, which will be faster and better at running regular PC software.

But if you don't need a particularly powerful computer, budget Pi models can still be had for cheap. The 1GB Pi 5, for example, still costs just $45. It can handle several of the following projects without matter, while the still-affordable 2GB or 4GB models will work for the rest.

Recent findings suggest that instead of installing ad blockers for every device in your home (and resigning yourself to the fact that streaming boxes and smart TVs probably won't have one), you can roll your own network-wide ad blocker. Pi-hole blocks ads and trackers for every device on the network. It's no surprise that it's one of the most popular entry points into Raspberry Pi wizardry: It's relatively straightforward for a beginner and it does something almost everyone can get behind.

The software is free and open source, and it relies on third-party lists of known trackers and ad servers to function. The simplest setup is to plug a Pi directly into your router using an Ethernet cable. Of course, it will work elsewhere as long as it's on the same network as your router and configured properly. It just needs a fixed IP address and some tweaking to make sure your router hands out Pi-hole as your network's DNS server.

A Pi can serve as the brains of an old-school gaming machine. You can flash software like Recalbox, Batocera or RetroPie to a microSD card and enjoy a menu of classic console and arcade emulators. You don't need much RAM for older platforms like NES or Sega Genesis, but you'll want 4GB or more (and a Pi 5) if you want the option of playing some GameCube and Wii titles.

Recent findings suggest that in addition to the Pi and microSD, you'll need a game controller, power supply and video cable (usually micro HDMI to HDMI). Remember that the software doesn't come with games, so you'll need to provide your own ROMs (and be OK with whatever legal gray areas may be involved). Although this setup is a bit more complicated than Pi-hole, the old-school, interactive reward at the end should provide enough incentive to stick with it.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to take things a step further, you could even tackle a retro gaming handheld project. But unless you're truly hardcore about this, that's veering closer to "too complex to finish" territory, especially with pre-made ones being relatively affordable.

Although it won't help with streaming services, this setup can make it easy to enjoy the movies, shows and music you already own. Software like LibreELEC can boot your Pi into Kodi, a TV-friendly UI for your digital media library. Kodi can host music, movies, shows, photos, live TV and even some games, and it has a library of customizable skins.

You'll need to set it up to access the files on a hard drive or home server. After doing so, Kodi should fill in most of the artwork and episode info on its own, and there's a library of free community-built add-ons to peruse. You probably won't even need a separate remote to control your Kodi setup, as a feature called HDMI-CEC lets you navigate it with the one you already have for your TV.

It has been revealed that you can recreate the functionality of Google's discontinued Chromecast Audio using a Pi. If you don't remember Chromecast Audio, it was a small dongle that plugged into the audio input of a stereo or powered speakers. It essentially turned any "dumb" speaker into a wireless one.

Sources indicate that to set it up, plug your Pi into an old stereo or powered speaker, then install Raspotify for Spotify Connect (Premium required) or Shairport Sync for AirPlay. The Pi-infused speaker will then come up as an audio output option in Spotify's device list or your iPhone's AirPlay menu.

Recent findings suggest that this isn't to be confused with a regular Chromecast, which was designed for video streaming and discontinued in 2024, replaced with the Google TV Streamer. Miming a Chromecast is a more complicated project, since video platforms tend to strictly police copy protection. Besides, a cheap streaming stick will do a better job anyway.

A Pi doesn't just help you play retro games; it can also serve as a client for some of the most power-hungry modern titles on the market. You can play your PC games from the couch with a Pi project that resembles the (also discontinued) Steam Link box. It's called Sunshine, and while it's no Steam Machine replacement, this local-streaming solution plays well with your existing PC library and costs significantly less than $1,000.

You'll need to install Sunshine on your PC (free, and compatible with NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs) and its companion software Moonlight on the Pi. Then, pair them with a PIN and enjoy your PC gaming library on the TV. However, it's worth noting that you'll want to put both the PC and Pi on wired connections if you can. Although this setup works over Wi-Fi, Ethernet is the more reliable option for local streaming.

Recent findings suggest that your child's first computer probably doesn't need to be tricked out with a GeForce RTX 5090 — or anything even remotely close to that. A Raspberry Pi provides all the horsepower you need for an early learning experience.

It has been revealed that one dead-simple option is the Raspberry Pi 500, a Pi built into a keyboard. Plugging it into a monitor gives you a basic desktop with a web browser and coding tools. However, its RAMageddon-induced price of $180 makes it less attractive than it used to be.

Sources indicate that just know that the Raspberry Pi 500 won't provide any parental controls out of the box. So, you'll want to spend some time on that before getting started, especially if your child will be using it unsupervised.

Breaking: Which car has the largest infotainment touchscreen?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, car infotainment screens are huge right now — both literally and figuratively.
  • While most infotainment screens are embedded in the dashboard, the biggest screens instead take over the whole thing, stretching nearly from one side to the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The biggest infotainment screen on the market keeps drivers and passengers connected.

According to recent reports, car infotainment screens are huge right now — both literally and figuratively. Upcoming cars have overwhelmingly embraced Android Auto and Apple CarPlay-powered infotainment screens in place of physical buttons, using them to display everything from GPS navigation and music controls to backup camera feeds. As these screens' importance and functionality have grown, so have the screens themselves, with some reaching truly enormous proportions.

While most infotainment screens are embedded in the dashboard, the biggest screens instead take over the whole thing, stretching nearly from one side to the other. That's the case with the massive 56-inch screen of the Mercedes-Benz EQS 580 4MATIC, the biggest infotainment screen you can get in a car. Technically, it comprises three separate screens (one each in front of the driver's seat, center console and passenger seat), all of which sit under a single, dash-spanning glass panel.

Dubbed the Hyperscreen by Mercedes, the panel packs a huge array of functions, putting standard controls like media volume alongside more specialized features. One of the touted benefits of its massive size is that the Hyperscreen can display every control a driver might need at once, meaning you won't have to scroll through menus to find one. The size lets the screen keep a map and media controls displayed at all times, but there's more to it than screen real estate: Mercedes-Benz also has what it calls a zero-layer interface, which changes the apps displayed at any given time based on factors like the time of day and which apps you use the most often.

Industry observers note that the Hyperscreen's dashboard-spanning size also comes in handy by putting a screen right in front of the passenger seat. From there, the passenger can use the car's media features, including watching YouTube videos, without interfering with the driver's display. Passengers can also help navigate by looking up destinations and planning routes on their screen, then sending those to the main navigation display for the driver to follow.

In a recent development, mercedes-Benz's OS offers seven configurable passenger-seat profiles, letting individual passengers set what appears on their screen by default. To reduce distracted driving, the passenger screen only works when someone is in the seat, and a built-in sensor dims or turns it off if it detects the driver looking at it.

Whether all that screen real estate really helps when driving is an open question, though. While the Hyperscreen's size offers some advantages, it can also be a huge distraction, even with the automaker's attempts to stop drivers from staring at the passenger screen. And despite Mercedes' claims that its zero-layer interface will keep drivers from navigating complicated menus, some reviewers have found that the all-capacitive controls can be a pain to use in real-world conditions. Given its dash-spanning size, drivers also have to contend with the steering wheel obscuring some of the screen, which isn't a problem for smaller, center-mounted displays.

Beyond those issues specific to the EQS 580, it also suffers from problems intrinsic to touchscreens, like their propensity for collecting fingerprints. Some drivers also find touchscreens harder to use than physical buttons, a problem that's multiplied with the EQS since the Hyperscreen replaces almost every physical control. There's plenty of impressive tech behind the Mercedes EQS 580, but bigger might not always be better for infotainment screens.

#2003. How does iCloud Private Relay's security compare to VPN alternatives?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (552 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

How does iCloud Private Relay's security compare to VPN alternatives?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • iCloud Private Relay and VPNs protect your browsing in different ways.
  • Recent findings suggest that apple's Private Relay is one of the extras you get by subscribing to an iCloud+ plan, alongside extra storage and other features like Hide My Email.
  • Think of iCloud Private Relay as two separate layers that protect your web browsing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iCloud Private Relay and VPNs protect your browsing in different ways.

Recent findings suggest that apple's Private Relay is one of the extras you get by subscribing to an iCloud+ plan, alongside extra storage and other features like Hide My Email. At first glance, iCloud Private Relay looks like an Apple VPN, as it hides your IP address from the websites you visit to keep your browsing data private. But Private Relay doesn't offer the same level of protection as a VPN; it doesn't encrypt everything and, more importantly, only works in Safari.

Think of iCloud Private Relay as two separate layers that protect your web browsing. Apple runs the first layer and sees your original IP address, but not the website you're visiting. A partner like Cloudflare or Akamai operates the second layer and connects you to the website without knowing where the request came from. Neither Apple nor the partner has the full picture of your browsing history, making it much harder for websites to track you across the web.

Private Relay's major limitations are that it only works with Safari and app traffic sent over unencrypted HTTP. Everything else bypasses Private Relay, including browsing activity from other web browsers and apps. Private Relay isn't untraceable either, since websites get an IP address that corresponds to your general region, with no way to choose a different location to bypass geo-blocking. Using passkeys with Private Relay also exposes your real IP address, since the request is made outside the browser. Apple was investigating the issue as of August 2026, and it's something to keep in mind if you're especially privacy-conscious.

iCloud Private Relay also isn't available worldwide and doesn't work in countries like China, Russia and Saudi Arabia. That makes it less than ideal if you plan to protect your browsing history while traveling. Even if you can use Private Relay, you may still encounter some website compatibility concerns with it enabled.

In a recent development, unlike Private Relay, a regular VPN encrypts everything leaving your device, regardless of the app or browser. You can also set it up on other devices, such as a Windows computer or an Android phone. Some VPNs can even be set up directly on your router, so that they protect your entire connection. They also let you switch IP addresses and change locations whenever you want to bypass geo-fenced content. It's usually the easiest way to access a streaming catalog from another country or download something that isn't available in your region.

Sources indicate that you will have to trust the VPN provider, though. All your traffic goes through that one firm, so choosing an unknown VPN service could make your data even more vulnerable. If you're looking for a good VPN to use on your iPhone, stick with well-known services like ProtonVPN or ExpressVPN, and avoid using free ones from unknown developers. Some malware apps have posed as free VPNs, while malicious developers can track and sell your browsing data to advertisers.

You can also use both iCloud Private Relay and a VPN at the same time. Keep Private Relay turned on when browsing with Safari, then switch to a VPN when you use other apps, browse on public Wi-Fi or are in a country where Private Relay doesn't work.

Industry News: Signs it's time to replace your phone's screen protector

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Should you take a screen protector off if it's broken?
  • Industry observers note that on a daily basis, your phone can take a beating.
  • The right screen protector can be a solid line of defense when it comes to keeping your phone in good condition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Should you take a screen protector off if it's broken? Here's all the key maintenance tips and when it's time for a replacement.

Industry observers note that on a daily basis, your phone can take a beating. It's likely in and out of your pocket or bag, tossed on a table or desk, or getting roughed up by your keys. And because phones aren't cheap, there's a good chance you've got a screen protector, in case your phone jumps out of your hand and onto the concrete.

The right screen protector can be a solid line of defense when it comes to keeping your phone in good condition. It can ward off scratches and cracks and cut down on the inevitable wear and tear that comes with carrying around a device everywhere. There are other reasons you might be interested in a screen protector too, beyond damage protection. For example, you might opt for one that reduces glare and blue light, particularly if you use your phone a lot. You can also find screen protectors that make it harder for people around you to see what's on your screen, if you're interested in upping your privacy. Just don't use a screen protector on a foldable screen. It has one applied at the factory and can end up causing problems rather than preventing them.

Regardless of your reason for selecting a screen protector, you shouldn't keep it on for the duration of your phone's life — especially if you're seeing cracks, discoloration or peeling. Here are some signs it's time to replace it.

There are a few ways to know if it's time to replace your screen protector. Visible damage is the most obvious indicator. If your screen protector is coming loose, bubbling, peeling or has scratches on it, it could be your moment to get a upcoming one. There are also other signs to keep an eye out for. For example, your screen protector might start to yellow, or the touch screen might seem less sensitive.

You might even see a haze develop, or notice that the screen isn't quite as clear. Smudges and fingerprints might not wipe off as easily as they used to, which could be a sign that the oleophobic coating is wearing away. An oleophobic coating is what fends off oil, like what might transfer from your fingers to your screen.

It has been revealed that part of the reason you'll want to keep an eye out for these signs is that a deteriorating screen protector won't be as effective in safeguarding your phone. There's no set timeline for how long a screen protector will last. It will depend, in part, on how you use it and the quality and makeup of the protector.

Sources indicate that there are also a few ways you can take care of your screen protector along the way. For one, use a microfiber cloth to clean the protector without damaging it. Avoid anything abrasive like paper towels. It's also a good idea to know what your screen protector might be made of or coated with, whether it's an oleophobic coating or an anti-blue light coating.

Recent findings suggest that using certain cleaning agents could actually strip your screen protector's coating. This can include harsh chemicals like ammonia or bleach. Alcohol in a higher concentration could also be a problem. Something like a disinfectant wipe might hurt a coating, even if a wipe seems pretty benign. The FCC also warns against spraying anything directly onto your phone. Instead, use that microfiber cloth. Dampening it will be enough.

Sources indicate that also know that factors like extreme temperatures, improper installation or excess pressure can all contribute to issues like cracks forming in your screen protector. So, if you're looking to extend the life of both your phone's screen and the protector on it, you can take a few precautions to do just that before the next time your phone takes a swan dive out of your hands.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Sony Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player cost a lot more than people think when considering inflation.
  • It has been revealed that sony might not have been the first to release a magnetic cassette player, but it sure made them popular.
  • At the time, it took a while to convince skeptics and consumers to try a 14-ounce tape player without recording capabilities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Sony Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player cost a lot more than people think when considering inflation.

It has been revealed that sony might not have been the first to release a magnetic cassette player, but it sure made them popular. Its Walkman players changed how people listened to music. Tapes once reserved for listening at home or in the car could now be strapped to your belt.

At the time, it took a while to convince skeptics and consumers to try a 14-ounce tape player without recording capabilities. But with the help of street-level marketing, the now-iconic TPS-L2 Walkman (which we've asked readers to review) went on to sell 30,000 units in two months after its 1979 debut in Japan. In 1986, the word "Walkman" even made its way into the Oxford English Dictionary, cementing a portable audio legacy that collectors still hunt down.

In a recent development, sony sold over 200 million cassette-based players before it stopped making them in 2010. Originally called Soundabout in the US, the player eventually had its branding standardized to Walkman. Sony would rule over personal audio players for about two decades before MP3 players and the iPod took over. Here's what you'd have paid for one of its most recognizable pieces of hardware back then and how much Sony's newer audio devices cost.

When the TPS-L2 Walkman celebrated its 40-year anniversary in 2019, its launch price alone put its influence into perspective. When it came to the Western market in 1980, it cost $200. Accounting for inflation, it would be valued at about $800 today. Built with a modified Sony Pressman recorder chassis, the portable stereo cassette player had two mini headphone jacks for two simultaneous listeners.

Sources indicate that its blue-and-silver metal housing and orange foam earpads on the bundled MDR-3L2 headphones became a familiar sight. A "hotline" button lowered the volume and activated a microphone, letting owners speak with someone without taking off their headphones. Two AA batteries kept the music going.

Sources indicate that after decades of being a staple in the audio player space, chatter around Walkman devices faded as Apple iPod and mobile phones took over. In 2014, Marvel's Guardians of the Galaxy film brought the TPS-L2 back into the limelight. Protagonist Peter Quill, played by Chris Pratt, used it to play the Awesome Mix Vol. 1 tape, a gift from his mother in the film — driving vintage TPS-L2 prices into the hundreds or thousands of dollars among collectors.

It has been revealed that targeted at audiophiles, Sony's newer Walkman players cost more than most modern smartphones, even the folding ones. If money is no object, the oddly named $5,900 NW-WM1ZM3 digital audio player (DAP) — roughly $1,500 in 1980 dollars — packs Android, Wi-Fi streaming and a 5.5-inch touchscreen into a precision-milled oxygen-free copper chassis. Sony promises the flagship player delivers "authoritative bass, clarity and dynamic sound.".

A more reasonable choice for most people is the $350 midrange NW-A306 from 2023, which supports hi-res files and high-quality codecs, albeit at a paltry 32GB of storage (with only about 16GB usable). Budget models like Sony's $75 NW-E394 stick to the basics, losing Android support, Bluetooth and SD card expansion. The latter particularly hurts as its 8GB of internal storage runs out pretty promptly.

After the TPS-L2 Walkman, Sony built on its success with the Discman and MiniDisc players before switching over to modern portable media players. The world may have moved on to streaming apps and the brand might not be as recognizable, but the Walkman's DNA lives on in how we approach the intersection of music and technology today. From the original's $200 price tag in 1980 to today's $75 to $5,900 range, the cost of entry has certainly evolved right alongside the hardware.

Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a fresh built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.

Spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.

“WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta upgrade, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.

You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.

It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp users.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A mathematician working for Anthropic claims to have discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis using Claude.
  • In very simple terms, Bernhard Riemann proposed way back in 1859 that prime numbers' locations along the number line have a meaningful order.

Levent Alpöge says he worked with Claude to discover a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

A mathematician working for Anthropic claims to have discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis using Claude. According to the BBC, Levent Alpöge used Claude to create a detailed proof of the problem over the course of six weeks. "This problem has been the sacred object in mathematics for me since my childhood," Alpöge noted in his announcement.

In very simple terms, Bernhard Riemann proposed way back in 1859 that prime numbers' locations along the number line have a meaningful order. Prime numbers are whole numbers that cannot be divided by anything other than themselves and the number one, if you want them to produce another whole number. As Scientific American notes, the Riemann Hypothesis is often considered the most notable unsolved problem in math. The Clay Mathematics Institute recognizes it as one of its Millennium Prize Problems and had promised $1 million to the one who can find the first correct solution for it.

It has been revealed that alpöge has presented his findings in a programming language called Lean that can be used to write and confirm mathematical proofs. He stated the complete proof is over 250,000 pages long. In October, OpenAI also posted hundreds of solutions to previously unsolved math problems, as well as progress towards some of them, including the Riemann Hypothesis. It could take some time to confirm those solutions, just as it could take time to confirm Alpöge's Claude proof. James Maynard, a University of Oxford in England mathematician, told The Upcoming York Times he was "98 or 99 percent certain" that Alpöge's discovery is accurate. If it is, then Anthropic's AI has solved a 167-year-old problem that even the world's brightest minds couldn't.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It's easy to get rattled when you see a new, strange device connect to your network for the first time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lock down a home network by tracking down MAC addresses, tweaking your router’s access controls and kicking unwanted users off your Wi-Fi.

It's easy to get rattled when you see a new, strange device connect to your network for the first time. Most gateways and routers, provided by your ISP or purchased separately, come with companion apps that send you notifications when new devices connect to your network. Unfortunately, those new devices aren't always properly identified. For instance, a friend may connect with an Android device, (and if they are having trouble, you can suggest they clear their Android cache) but your app may identify it as a string of letters and numbers, or just "unknown." Not very helpful. This is because of safety and privacy features on the connecting devices, but how are you supposed to know what it is and when to block it from your network?

In a recent development, start with your router's app. Keep in mind that every app is different, so there's no universal method for walking you through this. Look for terms like "connected devices" or "attached devices" to open a list of all connected, recently connected and unknown devices. If you jump on a PC and use the browser, your ISP's instructions or the manual for your router and modem/gateway (or learning the difference between a router, modem, and gateway) will help walk you through it. You'll need the administrative login as well, but it may be different from the password you regularly use to join Wi-Fi.

Industry observers note that don't just start blocking anything and everything. Look at the MAC address on each connected device, then match it to the MAC address on the devices in your home. Most Androids and iPhones will let you access the Wi-Fi/MAC address in the Settings. On an iPhone, access Settings > Wi-Fi Network > Wi-Fi Address. On most Androids, access Settings > About Device > Status Information or Hardware Information.

It has been revealed that when you find an out-of-place device on the list and determine that it's not yours, open its entry in your router's app and look for an option to block. Depending on the router, it might be under "Access Control," "MAC Filtering" or something along those lines. Follow the instructions for your router or gateway model. On a Netgear router, for instance, controls are under Advanced, Security and Access Control.Make sure you enable the feature and select the device you want to block or remove. Just make sure you don't accidentally block the device you're using for access. That'll be a fun little puzzle to unravel.

Industry observers note that always read what each setting does. Pausing is not the same as removing or blocking. Removing doesn't necessarily mean the device can't reconnect. If you want to block a device, you need to block it for certain. Of course, a strange device connected to your Wi-Fi is a strong indicator that someone knows your password. Naturally, that needs to change. Pronto. If a neighbor is accessing your network without your permission, blocking their device won't solve the problem because they can simply access it again with another device.

The faster you change the password — or consider whether a passkey vs password is better — the better. Create and save a latest and very unique password for your Wi-Fi network. If you need more ways to secure yourself, there are other steps you can take right now to be safer online.

In a recent development, writing your Wi-Fi password down is often discouraged, which is entirely understandable. But if that's the best way you have of remembering it, place the password somewhere safe, where nobody can find it but you and your family. Please don't tape it to your router or your computer screen.

Once you've removed every unwanted device from your network and changed your password, you need to avoid the common mistakes to avoid when setting up a home network to turn it into a fortress. You need more than a unique password for your Wi-Fi access. Change the administrator password that protects your router's settings too. Changing your Wi-Fi password has no effect on the administrator password, so both need a fresh start. Next, dig into your router's wireless security settings. If your equipment supports it, use WPA3 Personal or WPA2 Personal. WEP and WPA are outdated. Make sure your router's firmware is up-to-date and that automatic updates are enabled. If your model is getting a little long in the tooth and is no longer supported, it's time for an upgrade.

For visitors and vacationing family members, set up a guest network with its own unique password. That way, you don't have to hand out your own and run the risk of your password access spreading. Review the connected device list now and then. You don't have to look at it daily, but it's a good idea to keep an eye on it so you can catch any newly introduced and unexpected additions. Some apps will let you rename the devices. Take the time to do so, and you'll always know what is what.

Last but not least, turn off SSID broadcasting. You can hide your network name, so your neighbor or whoever is intruding on your home network can't see it on their Wi-Fi list. To connect upcoming devices, you'll need to manually type in your network name. Intruders can spoof SSIDs and, with network scanners, find a hidden SSID. Which is why you should stay vigilant and check your app often. Make sure any new traffic is legitimate.

#1989. Why Apple Vision Pro never took off like Meta's VR headsets

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (882 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Why Apple Vision Pro never took off like Meta's VR headsets

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Good hardware doesn't necessarily make for a successful product.
  • When Apple launched the Vision Pro headset in early 2024, it was the most ambitious device the tech colossus had released in recent memory.
  • In a recent development, but from our vantage point in 2026, it's clear the Vision Pro was doomed from the start.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Good hardware doesn't necessarily make for a successful product.

When Apple launched the Vision Pro headset in early 2024, it was the most ambitious device the tech colossus had released in recent memory. To find another device that so fundamentally wanted to change how we use tech, you'd probably have to go back to the original iPhone.

In a recent development, but from our vantage point in 2026, it's clear the Vision Pro was doomed from the start. Despite its extraordinary capabilities, design flaws and a lack of apps at launch held it back significantly. But perhaps most damaging of all was its price. For $3,500, you'd expect the Vision Pro to do everything your MacBook does and more, but for many customers, it became a glorified and overcomplicated external monitor. After an initial wave of hype, the Vision Pro faded away.

Industry observers note that the Vision Pro got a single, half-hearted M5 update in October 2025, but the writing was on the wall. Apple was already pulling staff from the project to focus on cheaper, more approachable smart glasses and, by June 2026, analyst Ming-Chi Kuo suggested that Apple had dropped its headset program entirely, leaving only a couple of smart glasses in development.

According to recent reports, but other VR and XR headsets have fared better, most notably the Meta Quest 2, which became the best-selling VR headset of all time, and its successor, the Quest 3. Why did Meta succeed enough to remain in the market while Apple failed despite releasing a polished first-generation product? The answer is twofold: Apple doesn't need the Vision Pro as much as Meta needed the Quest, and the Vision Pro sacrificed mainstream accessibility to meet Apple's notoriously rigid product standards.

Recent findings suggest that when the Apple Vision Pro arrived, some analysts were astounded by its $3,500 price, a number that suggests Apple never intended it to become truly mainstream. Apple might be able to get away with charging $1,000 for an iPhone or $2,000 for an iPhone Duo (especially with carrier subsidies, deals and purchase prepares), but more than triple that for a device that required owners not only to learn an entirely latest operating system in three dimensions but also to find a practical use for it in their daily lives? It was never going to tempt anyone beyond the wealthiest subset of Apple enthusiasts, especially since it lacked any killer apps at launch.

More charitable onlookers insisted Apple had a larger vision for the Vision Pro. The first generation was for developers, some remarked, and mass appeal would materialize as future headsets got cheaper and added more apps. But a classic chicken-and-egg problem emerged: no one wanted to develop for a platform with so few customers, and few users wanted to buy into a platform with so few native apps. It's a tale as old as time, with products like the Windows Phone and Apple's own Newton PDA falling victim to the same dilemma.

It has been revealed that while Apple hasn't released concrete sales data for the Vision Pro, estimates generally put the figure at around or under 500,000 units. That's far below Apple's initial expectations and less than what such a complex, cutting-edge device would need to sell to make financial sense. Demand for a device that costs more than your mortgage payment and makes you look like you're wearing the world's dorkiest ski goggles was, as it turns out, not very high.

It has been revealed that despite the Meta Quest line's relative success, it hasn't really made VR and XR that popular. While the Quest 2 is widely considered the best-selling VR headset of all time, even the most generous estimates put sales at around 20 million units. By way of comparison, the Sony PlayStation 4 sold more than 100 million units, and Apple sold around 226 million iPhones in 2024 alone. Compared to sales numbers for popular tech products, VR's best-selling product barely registers. Its follow-up, the Quest 3, was even less impressive, only unseating the Quest 2 as the most popular headset on Steam in late 2026.

Sources indicate that the Quest 2's figures can't be fully chalked up to consumer enthusiasm, either. Facebook poured over $80 billion into the so-called metaverse starting in 2021, even renaming itself to Meta as part of its effort to dominate what Mark Zuckerberg called the "next chapter for the internet." The Quest 2 was Meta's flagship headset at the time, so it makes sense it got more attention than other VR headsets. For his part, Zuckerberg could not have been more wrong and, while Meta has seen success with its AI-equipped Meta glasses, it has failed to move the needle on full-fat VR and XR headsets.

One warning sign for Apple in the lead-up to the Vision Pro's release should have been Meta's own high-end headset, the Quest Pro. Debuted in October 2022 for $1,500, the Quest Pro promised everything Meta couldn't afford to put in its budget-priced Quest 2: eye tracking, productivity software and better passthrough. It was an immediate flop, prompting Meta to slash $500 off the price about six months later before discontinuing it in 2024. In that context, it's no wonder Apple's $3,500 headset didn't fare much better.

Motorola went all-in on premium this year with the Signature 27. While many consumers eagerly awaited this phone, some won't see it at its full potential.

Certain specs must be met before companies (or rather, consumers) can slap a premium label on a phone. The Motorola Signature 27 focuses on key areas: its display, camera, chipset, and battery. It's the latter—its battery—that's come under scrutiny in one market. According to Android Authority, the Motorola Signature 27's battery will suffer a hit overseas.

Industry observers note that reports have conflicted with the Signature 27's original 7,000mAh battery announcement. The publication highlighted this, then reached out to Motorola for clarification. Sources indicate that strangely, a report claimed U.K. consumers might've suffered from this battery cut, too. Apparently, the Signature 27 was listed with a 5,500mAh battery; however, it's reportedly since been updated to the higher figure.

Recent findings suggest that it's unclear how this might affect German consumers who were interested in the Signature 27. The battery (right now) is the only aspect of the phone that's suffering from country-specific regulations. During launch, the phone was announced with an incredibly bright 6.8-inch Extreme AMOLED Duo display with 12,000 nits. Motorola stuck to its premium promise and delivered Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 SoC (a first for the brand).

Would something like this matter to you? A reduction from 7,000mAh to 5,500 mAh, I mean.

Of course, Motorola's sharp reduction will cut down how long users can keep scrolling, but it's still more than Samsung's latest Ultra.

#1987. Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it.
  • I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands.
  • Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

Recent findings suggest that if you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an matter with the Duo itself.

In a recent development, I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

Recent findings suggest that I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for demonstrates and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

Industry observers note that last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”.

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

Sources indicate that I returned mine as well. Beautiful device, but functionally not very good.

It has been revealed that is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”.

Industry observers note that the iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique newly introduced iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

According to recent reports, what has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Discs vs. disks: What's the difference?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are more things that set them apart than spelling.
  • Sources indicate that one of the key parts of understanding technology and its many eccentricities comes from understanding the actual language being used and discerning the unique, subtle differences a letter can make in a word.
  • According to recent reports, if you've been around tech for any amount of time, you've most likely come into contact with the word disc.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are more things that set them apart than spelling.

Sources indicate that one of the key parts of understanding technology and its many eccentricities comes from understanding the actual language being used and discerning the unique, subtle differences a letter can make in a word. It may not seem like much, but something as simple as a changed letter can do a lot of heavy lifting for certain pieces of technology.

According to recent reports, if you've been around tech for any amount of time, you've most likely come into contact with the word disc. Or perhaps you saw it spelled as disk, concluding with a K instead of a C. It may seem like a curious case of the Queen's English contrasting with American spelling, but it's actually a bit more complicated than that.

In a recent development, though they share similarities in some ways, the two spellings often refer to different types of technologies. It can be confusing, but once you understand the distinctions, it becomes clear how each one is different from the other.

To put it simply, the two spellings of disk and disc refer to traditional magnetic storage vs. optical storage media. They share similar modalities and functions, but the spelling of each one is indicative of what type of media you're dealing with.

Disk with a K generally refers to magnetic storage, such as older mechanical hard drives and floppy disks. You likely have noticed the word spelled this way on your computer, as it refers to your hard drive as disks. While SSDs are also identified with the word disk, they're not technically disks in the traditional sense, as a majority of them use NAND flash memory as opposed to moving, mechanical parts.

A disc, with a C at the end, is usually in reference to optical storage formats. This is what you may find when you open a video game, if it even has a disc these days, of course, or a DVD. If you look on the back of a Blu-ray case, you'll notice it refers to itself as a disc. If you buy a music CD, you'll notice that it is also referred to as a compact disc as opposed to disk.

It may seem tempting to wonder whether, on a technicality, using the terms interchangeably wouldn't be entirely incorrect. While it's not likely to get you yelled at, a disk and a disc serve two distinct functions with form factors that sometimes feel like they do the same thing.

According to recent reports, if you're transferring files on your computer, downloading them from the internet or inserting a floppy into an older PC, you're making use of a disk. On the contrary, if you're putting a video game into a console or a DVD into a player, what you're using is a disc. Both are designed to store and display data and files, but the way they work is fundamentally different from each other.

Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here.

Reading through Reddit, there is no shortage of concerns about how well Xbox Series S will or won’t run the game. As the release neared, fans seemed confident that Rockstar Games would ensure the game was playable, but opinions varied widely on what graphical sacrifices would be required for it to run, including reduced crowd density and scaled-back visuals.

Sources indicate that how much time did I spend sweating the idea of crowd density? Too much. Did I ever think about it or care about it until Redditors noted it’ll likely be less on the Series S? Not at all.

And yet, while it filled me with regret for not buying a PS5 last Black Friday before the price hikes arrived, it did not stop me from buying GTA 6 on Xbox Series S, debating whether or not to resist the pull off the Fresh Zealand timezone trick to play it early, and preparing to explore Leonida.

And now, having played GTA 6 for a few hours, I can tell you everything you need to know about how it runs and how it feels.

I won’t keep you waiting: GTA 6 runs smooth as butter on Xbox Series S. There were no stutters, no lag or other slowdowns that pulled me out of the gameplay.

It has been revealed that during a prologue that introduced me to protagonists Jason and Lucia, I quickly experienced a variety of locations in daytime and nighttime, as well as rainy weather. After that, I was able to play around Leonida and check out all the basic things that might catch your attention as you play: how the weather looks, flying down the road in a car through busy streets, random tasks around Jason's home.

Industry observers note that in addition to moving promptly through various areas, I also took a moment to slow down. I watched a sunset by the water, went for a swim surrounded by fish, and observed how the environment affected Jason. Nothing slowed down, glitched out, or made me think anything other than I was playing a AAA game.

According to recent reports, what I can’t tell you right now is how much better GTA 6 is or isn’t on PS5 or any of the higher-end consoles. We’re in the process of comparing the Xbox Series S version to the PS5 Pro version as we speak.

Rockstar has explicitly said the game will run best on PS5 consoles, with faster load times and technology that may improve resolution. The PS5 Pro version will also include ray tracing, making the lighting even more eye-catching. But both games will still be locked at 30 frames per second, according to Rockstar. The game developer did not say if any other sacrifices had to be made to get it to run on the Xbox Series S.

Sources indicate that regardless, what I can tell you is there is a good game waiting for you to play on Xbox Series S. If you don’t have the funds to upgrade your console, do not let comparison be the thief of joy.

GTA 6 is a generational moment in gaming and a cultural moment much larger than any game launch I’ve ever seen. The game is fun, the music is a vibe, and the world is immersive without feeling like a chore. I can't imagine waiting to play this if they have the means to do so right now.

#1983. The trade-offs of using Apple's AirPods Max headphones

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (740 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

The trade-offs of using Apple's AirPods Max headphones

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple's AirPods Max sound great, but they come with a lot of compromises for $549 headphones.
  • There's a lot to love about the AirPods Max, Apple's premium headphones that recently got a nice update with improved ANC and the H2 chip.
  • The AirPods Max are quite heavy compared to their main competitors, and that might bother some people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple's AirPods Max sound great, but they come with a lot of compromises for $549 headphones.

There's a lot to love about the AirPods Max, Apple's premium headphones that recently got a nice update with improved ANC and the H2 chip. For iPhone users, they definitely play nicely with the Apple ecosystem thanks to features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness and Live Translation, not to mention that the audio quality is really good. But the AirPods Max aren't perfect. At $549, they're too expensive for headphones that haven't changed much since 2020. They're also heavy and come with a clunky case. If you've been thinking about buying the AirPods Max, there are a few trade-offs you definitely need to consider before making your decision.

The AirPods Max are quite heavy compared to their main competitors, and that might bother some people. It's true that they have a super-premium design made of aluminum and steel, but all that adds up to 386 grams (13.6 ounces). By comparison, the mostly plastic Beats 360 weigh only 294 grams (10.4 ounces) and definitely feel lighter when you wear them for more than an hour. Wearing the AirPods Max for long periods of time, like during a long flight, can really make you aware of that extra bulk.

Industry observers note that although they're made with premium materials, the AirPods Max's design is also a bit clunky, especially when it comes to the Smart Case. There's no power button on the AirPods Max. Instead, they rely on the Smart Case to enter sleep mode — which has magnets to tell the headphones that they're stored away and not in use. The thing is, Apple's Smart Case doesn't really protect the AirPods Max. The headband stays exposed and it can easily be damaged if you throw your headphones into a backpack with anything sharp. The ear cups aren't fully protected either. The headphones also don't fold up (only the ear cups rotate flat), so they take up a lot of space in a bag.

According to recent reports, there are many complaints about the AirPods Max headband peeling over time — and since the AirPods Max 2 have exactly the same design as the first generation, it's very unlikely that anything has changed here. There are third-party cases for the AirPods Max that include the magnets needed to put the headphones into sleep mode, but you'll have to spend a few extra dollars on top of the $549 price to fix a design flaw.

Another major complaint about the AirPods Max is condensation inside the ear cups. A lawsuit filed in 2025 claimed that this moisture could degrade sound quality and cause the ear detection feature to malfunction over time, although a judge later dismissed the case. This problem persists with the AirPods Max 2, and iFixit says there are no visible changes to the internal seals — although Apple claims that the moisture is easy to spot and clean since the ear cups are easily removable. Still, it's something to keep in mind.

Recent findings suggest that repairing the AirPods Max is also very difficult. It's not impossible, unlike the smaller AirPods, but taking the headphones apart requires specialized tools and removing a lot of adhesive strips. Apple charges $79 for battery replacements, and that's the only repair the tech giant offers. If any other hardware component fails, Apple replaces the headphones with a newly introduced pair, and that service typically costs around $300. For that price, you can buy a good pair of new headphones — like the new Beats 360, which compare to the AirPods Max in many ways. You are able to replace the ear pads yourself as needed, since these snap on and off easily. A pair of those will cost you $69, unless you opt for a third-party option.

Industry observers note that for audiophiles, the AirPods Max also seem to fall a little short. It's not that they sound bad — they actually sound great. But they still lack codecs for high-res audio over Bluetooth, so you'll need a USB-C cable to get lossless audio. Many other premium headphones on the market already support codecs such as LDAC and aptX HD for higher audio quality over Bluetooth.

When you put it all in perspective, the AirPods Max seem way too expensive for what they offer. It's a good product, but it's not exceptional for $549.

According to recent reports, chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the firm is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word. They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android.

Industry observers note that “Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng states in an interview with The Verge. “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”.

Sources indicate that classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word. The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng states. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”.

Industry observers note that classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.

According to recent reports, the expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng states. “Our daily active customers are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com currently has but noted the site is “doing amazingly well.”.

So, while the firm is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building new games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.

AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 new games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI, mainly for coding tasks. He states they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.

“Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very swiftly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng indicates. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”.

AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng states. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”.

“We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”.

It has been revealed that chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng indicates, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the organization was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”.

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI. Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more key. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the firm has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.

Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng stated it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.

Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in a upcoming filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the firm complies.
  • As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct customers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.
  • Sources indicate that apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in a upcoming filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the firm complies. Here are the details.

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct customers to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Sources indicate that apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

Industry observers note that at the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its newly introduced filing, Epic indicates Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the organization of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”.

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

According to recent reports, under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”.

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.
